text:
The Monier-Williams half of the 2026-08 correction queue, split into its own PR because a 21,811-line diff should not ride inside a multi-dictionary batch. Companion to [#2884](https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-orig/pull/2884) (ap90 + mw72 + pwg). Auto-merge intentionally OFF.

| change | lines | issue | status |
|---|---:|---|---|
| wrap bare `&c.` as `<ab>&c.</ab>` | 21,791 (25,111 occurrences) | [MWS#86](https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/MWS/issues/86) | approved by @drdhaval2785, 2026-06-28 |
| phw cross-reference graph repair | 26 | H1500 | `phw_audit.py`: 0 issues, 2,369/2,369 edges 100% reciprocal (was 2,364 / 99.3% / 31 issues) |

Six lines carry both changes. They touch disjoint parts of the line, so the phw fix is applied first and the `&c.` rule then runs over the whole file — no special-casing.

## Relocated onto `main` before shipping — please read this bit

The queued change files were prepared against a **branch**, not `main`. Against `main`, **20,618 of 21,817 records failed**: five upstream July correction commits (`de8c1862`, `d649aee8`, `921c916f`, `54e06384`, `4b0fdecd`) net-deleted one line at 59923 and shifted every later line number by one. Applying them as staged would have corrupted the file.

Relocation was **not** a blind offset:

- `change_mw_1` is a **rule**, not a hand-list, so it was **regenerated** against `main` rather than shifted. Before substituting it, the rule was proven equivalent to the approved change file: it reproduces `change_mw_1` **byte-for-byte on that file's own base**, and fires on **exactly** the same lines (zero extra). So this is the approved change, re-derived — not a re-interpretation of it.
- `change_mw_2` is a hand-list, so its 26 records were relocated **by content**. Three of them share the body `¦ See <s>meTi</s><info lex="f"/>` and take **different** `phwparent` values; content alone would have collapsed them and written the wrong pointer into the wrong record. They were disambiguated by each record

title: chore(release): add 2.18 release announcements ahead of the cycle (Closes #1385)
text:
## Summary

Adds `RELEASE_ANNOUNCEMENTS["2.18"]` to `ldm_core/constants.py`, ahead of
opening the v2.18.0 pre-release cycle.

Closes #1385. Refs #1384 (the cycle itself stays open).

## Why it must land first

`test_release_announcements_contract` derives its key from `VERSION`:

```python
v_prefix = ".".join(VERSION.split(".")[:2])
self.assertIn(v_prefix, RELEASE_ANNOUNCEMENTS, ...)
```

Series present today are `2.15`, `2.16`, `2.17`. The moment
`scripts/release.py --bump preminor` writes `2.18.0-pre.1`, a missing `2.18`
entry fails that test and the release CI goes red -- so this cannot ride along
with the bump.

## Contents

| Entry | Issues |
|---|---|
| `ldm run --search-mode shared` works end to end | #1353, #1362, #1363 |
| Remote node awareness before blocking | #1341 |
| Unreachable node diagnosis | #1345 |
| `ldm info` reports effective names | #1351 |
| Batch commands survive one failing project | #1343 |

Validated against the contract's shape rules: five non-empty 2-tuples, and the
existing test still passes at `VERSION = "2.17.0"`.

## Verification

The mandatory pre-flight gate from
`.agents/skills/release-orchestration/SKILL.md`:

```
.venv/bin/python3 -m pre_commit run --all-files   -> 17 hooks, 0 failures
mypy ldm_core --config-file=mypy.ini              -> 146 files, clean
```

`detect-secrets` failed on the first run and regenerated `.secrets.baseline`.
The diff was inspected rather than staged blindly: six `line_number` fields
shifted by exactly 26 -- matching the constants.py addition -- plus the
`generated_at` timestamp. No new secret entries, no new files.

## Note on the issue split

The first commit on this branch said `Closes #1384`, which would have closed
the release tracking issue while the release had not happened. Amended to close
#1385 instead, so #1384 closes on promotion via the tracking PR that
`scripts/release.py --issue 1384` creates.

title: Every gate stage's failure-decider needs a planted-defect row — two for two are uncovered
text:
## What is wrong

Two lanes, doing unrelated work, each found the same shape in the stage they happened to be editing: the
stage has exactly **one** function that decides whether a condition counts as a *failure* rather than a
footnote, and **no self-test exercises that decision**. Turning the refusal into a note left the whole
stage green.

| found by | the decider | measured consequence |
|---|---|---|
| #537 / PR #584 | `_e2e_runtime_failure` — the only function deciding whether a runtime timeout is a failure | the **entire e2e suite** stayed green |
| #585 / PR #595 | `sweep_check_total` — the only function deciding that a **truncated corpus** is a failure | `a64_sweep` stayed fully green: `selftest ok`, `match=310`, `no silent miscompiles` |

The second is the sharper one: a stage that can be made to *test nothing at all* while printing
`no silent miscompiles`. The nine-row synthetic self-test standing beside it passed throughout, because
it exercises the **comparison** and not the **verdict**.

This is a third generator under #470, distinct from the two that umbrella already names. The first two
are about what a stage *asserts*. This one is about whether the stage's **verdict machinery** is itself
asserted — a self-test suite can be complete about comparisons and still report green on a stage that a
refactor or a merge resolution has silently disarmed.

## The unit

Audit every gate stage for one question and close what the audit finds: **which function decides that a
condition is a failure, and is that decision exercised by a planted defect?** Two for two is enough to
assume the answer is "no" until measured.

The audit method is the one both lanes used, and it is cheap: plant a one-line change turning the
refusal into a note, run **that stage alone**, and see whether it goes green.

title: Show only stats that share a scope on the build footprint
text:
The rule showed **prompts, hours and tokens at equal weight** — but on a project built mostly in another tool, those three don't describe the same thing.

Milk Me Not's prompt count spans Lovable and Claude Code. Its hours and tokens cover the Claude Code portion alone, roughly a twentieth of the work. Three numbers side by side imply a parity the data doesn't have, and a caveat underneath doesn't undo it — the reader has already read them as peers.

## The stat set now follows what's known about each project

**Mixed-tool** (a hand-entered source exists):

> **2,512** prompts · **18** months
> *2,315 in Lovable (Feb 2025–Aug 2026), 197 in Claude Code. Hours and token counts aren't shown for this one: Lovable doesn't report them, so they'd describe only the smaller half of the work.*

**Fully measured** (unchanged):

> **318** prompts · **24.4** hours · **7.2M** tokens out
> *Measured from Claude Code, 2026-07-24 to 2026-08-21 — about 54% of this project's commits…*

## Two choices worth explaining

**Months, not a date range** — so the value still reads as a numeral like every other stat. It's derived from git, so it covers work in any tool, unlike hours which only exist where Claude Code logged a session. The exact range stays in the caveat.

**The caveat now explains the absence.** It previously said "hours and tokens cover the Claude Code portion only", describing figures no longer on the page.

## Commits were rejected as the third stat

The obvious candidate, and tool-agnostic — but folio has 26 commits for 318 prompts while Milk Me Not has 3,046 for 2,512. That fifteenfold spread reflects squashing versus per-change auto-commits, not effort. Side by side it would invite a comparison that means nothing.

## Verification

- `node build.js` in a clean `git archive` checkout **before** committing
- Both layouts confirmed rendering in the browser
- Staged by matching unique text rather than line numbers — the line-number approach is what broke master in #68
- Zero

title: Proposal: sort the open backlog
text:
Lane: default

## Goal

A written proposal gives every open `later` issue one outcome: close it, merge it into another issue, or keep it (in a proposed stage, or parked), as the two proposals on the big picture (#83, `docs/specs/2026-10-01-big-picture.md`) and on doc lifecycles (#84, `docs/specs/2026-10-01-doc-lifecycle.md`) describe. The owner decides on it afterwards.

## Background

The backlog has about 37 open issues, all labelled `later`, with no order, no grouping and almost no dependencies. 19 of them are one-line items copied from the v1 spec's "Not in v1" table; others are follow-ups of issues that are closed now. The research report `docs/research/big-picture-and-lean-docs.md` (section "The backlog as a graph, from the issue text alone") shows what is missing.

Both proposals (#83 and #84) are closed. Their files are on `main`. Both are still "owner decides", so this file uses them as a form to write in, not as accepted rules.

The form to use is in the section "Form of one issue's group, order and blockers" of `docs/specs/2026-10-01-big-picture.md`:

```
#<n> -> stage #<stage>, position <k>, blocked by <none | #<a>, owner/repo#<b>>
#<n> -> parked, source <URL>
```

No stage issue exists yet, and this work creates none. So in this file a proposed stage has a short name in place of `#<stage>`, for example `stage "Guard fixes"` (synthetic example).

text:
Plans the development line after 1.0.0, and removes from `PLAN.md` the roadmap that is already finished.

## PLAN.md: 1181 → 322 lines

The ten stage records that took SNACK from an empty repository to `1.0.0` move verbatim to `docs/history/roadmap-0.1-1.0.md`. They are archived rather than deleted because `docs/compatibility.md`, the ADRs, and the release notes all refer to those stages by number. `PLAN.md` keeps one line per version.

## The 1.x line, with no planned 2.0

Everything on the roadmap is additive or is human formatting, and human formatting is explicitly not a public contract under the policy 1.0 confirmed. Nothing here forces a major, so none is announced.

title: labs: derive the rev date from file mtime — the hand-typed half had drifted in all 9
text:
## What a "rev stamp" is

The small badge in the top-right of every lab:

```
rev 2026-08-04 14:18 · fp 567fb8
```

It exists because of your repeated "I'm not seeing the updates" reports. Two halves:

- **`fp`** — a fingerprint hashed from the page's actual script text at load. Reload; if it doesn't change, you're on a cached copy. **Derived, so it cannot lie.**
- **`rev`** — when the file last changed. **Typed by hand, so it can.**

## And it did — in every single lab

| lab | typed | actual mtime |
|---|---|---|
| bend-lab | 15:29 | 15:43 |
| width-lab | 08-02 18:20 | 08-03 00:02 |
| layout-lab | 18:20 | 21:03 |
| filter-lab | 07:55 | 14:15 |
| detune / ensemble / mod / reverb / shape | 18:58 | 19:01 |

**Nine for nine.** Same failure mode as ROADMAP's status lines (L0025): nothing forces the update when you edit, so the manual half rots while the derived half stays honest. A stale date inside the anti-staleness badge is worse than no date — it's the one place a wrong number actively misleads.

## The fix

`document.lastModified`, which works over `file://` and returns the file's real mtime. Nothing to remember, nothing to bump.

Caveat written into the code rather than left as a surprise: mtime is when *this copy* was written, so a `git checkout` of an unchanged file bumps it. That's still the right answer for the question the badge exists to answer — *is the browser showing what's on disk?* — just not "when the code last changed".

I had a one-line change staged that corrected filter-lab's number by hand. That was treating the symptom, so I discarded it in favour of this.

All 10 labs parse (checked each `<script>` block); `./verify fast` exit 0.

title: Diff viewer: keep tree folds, selection, cursor and base across reload/reopen (ZEN-233)
text:
Closes ZEN-233.

## Problem

`DiffViewerOverlay.apply(_:)` rebuilt the tree on every changed load and snapped back to fully-expanded + first-file-selected, discarding a collapsed directory or a mid-review cursor on the silent background refresh and on a base switch. The `NSOutlineView` holds its rows by object identity, so a rebuild can't inherit the old folds or selection.

## Change

- `DiffOutlineItem` gains a value `identity` (section title + path) that survives the rebuild.
- `apply` captures where the reader was (folded rows, open file, cursor line) before rebuilding and restores it after: folds re-close depth-first, the selection **follows its file even when a `git add` moves it Unstaged → Staged**, and the cursor lands back on its line by number (never index). A directory a load first shows comes up expanded, like any first-seen row.
- The cursor is carried across the async highlight swap via a new `restoringCursor:` on `DiffPaneTable.show`, reusing the existing `DiffSelection` line-number identity.
- `WindowController`'s two parallel per-repo caches (status + highlight store) fold into one `DiffViewerSession` that also carries the picked base and the reader's place, so **reopening ⌘D lands where you left off**. In memory only, one repo at a time; the overlay snapshots on teardown (`viewDidMoveToWindow` with no window), not per keystroke.

## Tests

- Interaction tests (real key events, window-mounted) for reload restore: folded directory stays folded, selected file + cursor survive a changed reload, selection follows a file staged mid-review, a vanished file falls back to the first, a first-seen directory opens, and full reopen restore (base + file + cursor + folds).
- Identity tests: stable across a rebuild from the same status; the same path in two sections gets two identities.
- Mutation-checked: reverting the restore fails all four core tests; reverted before commit.
- `bin/check` fully green (965 tests, format-lint + swiftlint clean).

## Follow-up

title: docs: record in the field, identify on the web (ADR 0011)
text:
Field records ([0008](https://github.com/padiush/platform/blob/main/docs/decisions/0008-specimens-and-determinations.md), [0009](https://github.com/padiush/platform/blob/main/docs/decisions/0009-collecting-permits.md), [0010](https://github.com/padiush/platform/blob/main/docs/decisions/0010-field-records-and-basis.md)) were built on the web and marked *"server-side this version."* That was a sequencing choice made when no field study was near — not a judgment about where a record belongs.

Almost everything a field record holds is known only while standing in front of the thing being recorded. The coordinates come from the device on the researcher's body; the photographs from the camera in their hand, and for an observation the photograph *is* the record; the collection number is being written on the tag at that moment; the vernacular name is being said out loud by the person beside them. Entering it on the web later means it was written on paper first — which is the transcription failure the companion was built to remove for interviews.

**And one moment the web cannot reach at all:** during an interview an informant names a plant and points at it. The answer and the record are the same event. `FieldRecord.instance_answer_id` — *"the answer this record came out of"* — is already in the model, and **nothing on the web uses it**. Not an omission; a seam waiting for the only device that can be present when both things happen at once.

### The decision

Extends [ADR 0003](https://github.com/padiush/platform/blob/main/docs/decisions/0003-capture-only-companion-scope.md) rather than reversing it. Its boundary is unmoved — design, linking, analysis and export stay on the web. What changes is that capture stops meaning only an interview. ADR 0008's own lifecycle draws the line:

| Stage | Authored by |
|---|---|
| **Recorded** — basis, vernacular name, collection number, coordinates, locality, notes, permit, photos and audio | **device** |
| **Identified** — determination

title: Delta-scoped semantic conflict detection ("dreaming" for a git-native workspace)
text:
**Part of:** #3

**What problem does this solve?**
Git (and #93's branch-per-agent conventions) detects *textual* conflicts — two edits touching the same lines. It has no concept of *semantic* conflicts: two edits that never touch the same line but jointly leave the workspace factually inconsistent (e.g. one document is updated to say a decision was reversed, a sibling document nobody touched still states the old decision as current). This is a real, distinct research problem, not a variant of the concurrency problem #93 addresses — solving concurrency perfectly still leaves this open, and vice versa.

Two lines of evidence say a semantic-conflict layer is worth building, and constrain how:
- **Anthropic's own "dreaming" architecture** (Lamis Mukta, AI Native DevCon talk; our own transcript via yt-dlp is the primary source, since no public transcript exists) — an orchestrator fans a fleet of sub-agents out across the *entire* memory store plus a batch of session transcripts, every cycle, to find drift and propose diffs for human approval. The speaker explicitly names the cost of this ("you might think, that sounds really expensive... [laughter]") and argues it pays for itself in fewer retries and shorter agent runs downstream — but the architecture re-reads everything each cycle because unstructured session transcripts carry no cheap signal for "what changed since last time."
- **SemanticCommit** (Vaithilingam, Kim, Acosta-Parenteau, Lee, Mhedhbi, Glassman, Arawjo; UIST 2025; DOI 10.1145/3746059.3747778; [arXiv:2504.09283](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09283)) is the one academic source that targets this exact surface — CLAUDE.md-style intent-specification documents, not code or structured data. It uses a knowledge-graph-based RAG pipeline to detect conflicts between new and existing content, presents them with confidence-colored UI (pink = ambiguous, red = requires attention), and offers resolution at both global (whole-document) and local (specific-passage) scope wit

title: fix(coding): keep coding runs out of the shared checkout, and let git-lfs repos push
text:
Refs #682. Fixes items 1, 2 and 4 of that issue. Item 3 (a committed fix marks a problem resolved) stays open there.

**What went wrong.** On 2026-09-24/25, four Sentry investigations on screener-p-server committed fixes, and none reached GitHub. The main checkout on meem was also left on a fix branch. One missing PATH entry caused all of it:

1. The worker runs git over a non-interactive SSH session, which skips the login profile. So `~/.local/bin`, where git-lfs lives, is not on the PATH.
2. screener-p uses Git LFS, so `git worktree add` failed at checkout.
3. `start_kimi_run` then fell back to launching the agent in the **shared checkout**. The agent (Claude Code, stockopedia account) created its branches there.
4. Later, `git push` failed in the LFS pre-push hook, so the approved PR never opened. The error was dropped, and the PR title came out as "fix: 1".

**Changes**
- `_exec` puts `$HOME/.local/bin` on the PATH for every remote command.
- A failed `worktree add` now fails the run. It no longer falls back to the shared checkout.
- After each run, `remove_worktree` puts the shared checkout back on its default branch, but only when it sits on an `aegis-fix/` branch with no uncommitted changes. A branch the user checked out, or uncommitted work, is never touched. The fix branch itself is kept for the PR.
- Both prompts that can commit (alert investigation and self-diagnose) carry one shared `GIT_HYGIENE` rule: commit only in the run's worktree, don't touch other checkouts, check `git status` before finishing, and put back anything changed, even on failure.
- `fix_pr_title` drops a leading list marker, so "1. In `group_as_list`…" no longer becomes "fix: 1".
- When no PR opens, the task note now gives each branch's error.

text:
Makes `/build-deck` answer the question it claimed to answer: *"best cards for commander X within budget Y"* — weighted by tournament wins, constrained by Commander Bracket, and with a total price that reflects what the deck actually costs.

Three commits, each builds standalone (verified with `git worktree` + full `dotnet build` per SHA, so `git bisect` works across the range).

---

## `f4ed638` — fix(ingestion): prices and large writes

Four data bugs, all of which fed into the deck builder.

**Scryfall retired the bulk-data contract.** `download_uri`/`size` are gone in favour of `jsonl_download_uri`/`compressed_size` (gzipped JSON Lines, not a JSON array). The old fields deserialised to empty string, the download resolved to `https://api.scryfall.com/` and 400'd — **startup ingestion had been failing outright**. The cache now decompresses on the way to disk and sniffs array-vs-JSONL when reading, so existing caches still load.

**Unpriced and mispriced printings made staples look free.** `default_cards` lists every printing and the index kept the first one seen — often a gold-bordered, memorabilia or digital printing with all-null prices. Combined with `PriceEur ?? 0m` in the builder, a "€100" deck was quietly stuffed with cards it could not afford:

text:
Gather's path from development to a production web app and store-distributed mobile app, with a staging build that exercises the production backend before store review.

## Decisions and constraints

title: Bring git-expert to parity with the language experts
text:
## Context

The language experts (`go-expert`, `rust-expert`, `python-expert`,
`js-ts-expert`, `zig-expert`, `php-expert`, `bash-expert`) now share one
shape: philosophy, modes named by a probe (`py-mode`, `sh-mode`,
`php-mode`, `js-mode`), a policy boundary between project mandate and
convention, a verification baseline backed by a tool (`sh-census`,
`php-census`), a `PLAYBOOK.md`, a `CODE-REVIEW.md` on the shared
`code-review` scale, and version awareness.

`git-expert` predates that work. Its `SKILL.md` is a commit-message
manual: it covers one Git verb (`commit`) and none of the operations an
agent actually gets wrong. It has no playbook, no review scenarios, no
probe, no gate, and it is not registered as a `code-review` extension.
Its `description` does not trigger on rebase, conflicts, bisect or
history rewriting.

## Findings on `skills/git-expert/SKILL.md` (review of 2026-09-14)

- **Autonomy contradiction:** "Feature Branches: can propose or even
  execute frequent commits" contradicts "No Auto-Commit". Autonomy is
  already owned by the engine environment modes (COUNSELOR / UNHINGED);
  the skill should not redefine it.
- **Wrong pre-commit diff:** `git diff HEAD` includes unstaged changes,
  so the review covers more than the commit. Pre-commit review must use
  `git diff --staged`.
- **Hardcoded branch name:** "Master Branch (The Sacred Line)" assumes
  `master`; the default branch must be detected (`main`, `trunk`,
  `origin/HEAD`).
- **Incomplete type list:** `chore`, `ci`, `build`, `perf`, `revert` and
  breaking changes (`!`, `BREAKING CHANGE:`) are missing; this repository
  already uses `chore`.
- **Convention stated as law:** lowercase titles and the 50-column title
  are conventions, not Conventional Commits requirements. They need a
  policy boundary like the language experts have.
- **Workflow coupling:** "MUST run `tw-flow status`" ties the skill to
  one workflow tool; the skill must degrade when it is absent.
- **Duplicated source of truth:*

title: Improve drupal-work-on-issue skill: 6 friction points from real-world use
text:
Background

  During a session working on issue #3576096, several friction points in the /drupal-work-on-issue skill surfaced.
  These are improvements to make the agentic workflow more robust and require less user intervention.

  ---

Fixes for https://github.com/mglaman/drupalorg-cli/blob/main/skills/drupal-work-on-issue/SKILL.md

  Issues and proposed fixes

  1. Directory detection should check CLAUDE.md first

  The skill runs git remote get-url origin to verify the working directory, but in a Drupal site the module lives at a
   subdirectory (e.g. web/modules/contrib/canvas), not the site root. If CLAUDE.md documents the module path, the
  skill should read it first and cd there automatically — only prompting the user if no guidance is found.

  2. Auto-select the branch when unambiguous

  The skill pauses to ask "which branch?" even when only one branch matching <nid>-* exists in the fork. If there is
  exactly one candidate, it should be selected automatically. Only prompt if there are multiple candidates or none.

  3. Replace git add -p with non-interactive staging

  git add -p is an interactive command that breaks in agentic contexts. Step 4 should stage only the specific files
  the agent modified:
  # instead of:
  git add -p

  # use:
  git add <specific-changed-files>

  4. Infer commit message style from git log

  The hardcoded template Issue #<nid> by <username>: <short description> doesn't match projects using conventional
  commits. The agent should run git log --oneline -5 before drafting a commit message and match the project's style.

  5. Handle the no-MR-exists case

  When mr:list returns no MRs, the skill currently tries to inspect files/diff/status on nothing. Instead it should:
  - Clearly report "No MR exists yet"
  - Skip the MR inspection steps
  - After the first push, capture the GitLab MR-creation URL that appears in the git push output and surface it to the
   user
  - Re-run mr:list after push to pick up the newly created MR I

title: feat: add split-commits skill for atomic commit-chunking
text:
## Summary

Adds a **`split-commits`** skill that breaks an uncommitted working tree spanning multiple tasks into one logical, atomic commit per concern — instead of a single mixed commit.

- **`.claude/skills/split-commits`** — survey the tree, cluster changes by *intent*, propose an ordered Conventional-Commit plan, and (only after approval) stage and commit each group.
- **Path-level grouping** by default; **hunk-level splitting** when one file mixes concerns, done non-interactively (interactive `git add -p`/`-i` isn't available in this harness) via `git diff -U0 -- <file>` → keep the concern's `@@` blocks → `git apply --cached --unidiff-zero`. Falls back to committing the file whole (with a flag) when concerns can't be cleanly separated.
- **`AGENTS.md`** — makes it the default: any commit spanning >1 concern is split, always behind an approval gate (never auto-commit). `CLAUDE.md` inherits this via `@AGENTS.md`.
- Safety: refuses the default branch and mid-rebase; commits the staged subset only (never `git commit -a`); records the pre-split HEAD so the whole thing is undoable with `git reset --soft`.

Counterpart to the `doc-sync` orchestrator (PR #2): where doc-sync keeps docs truthful, split-commits keeps history legible.

## Test plan

- [x] Non-interactive hunk-split validated in a scratch repo, **including the failure mode**: default 3-line context coalesces changes within ~6 lines into one hunk, so `-U0` is required to separate them.
- [x] End-to-end flow validated (2 whole-file concerns + 1 mixed file → 2 atomic commits): each commit contained only its concern's hunks; tree ended clean; `git reset --soft` restored all changes.

title: Add the gtb-git-commit-conventions skill
text:
Adds `gtb-git-commit-conventions` and the eval suite that exercises it, building on the shared seeding helper from #15.

The skill covers **when** to commit and **how to scope** a commit, not only how to write the message — the division of work into commits is decided while the work happens, so it loads at the start of a session rather than when a commit is imminent. Sections: commit cadence and atomicity, message shape (subject grammar, wrapping, why-not-how), trailers, `--fixup`/`--autosquash`, `git revert`, and the GPG signing indicator.

## Naming

Named with a `gtb-` prefix, which the existing skills don't have yet.

Skills installed by the `skills` CLI land flat in `.claude/skills/`, keyed on the directory name — there's no namespace layer. (The `plugin:skill` form you see for plugin-sourced skills is composed by the harness at load time from the plugin name; it isn't part of a skill's own name.) So a generic name collides silently: a project-level `git-commit-guidelines` from an employer's repo and a user-level one from dotfiles shadow each other, with no signal about which loaded — and they'd disagree about exactly the things this skill is opinionated on.

`gtb-` matches the existing `gtb` CLI and `@gtbuchanan/*` scope, so it reads as ownership. A colon (`gtb:`) isn't an option: Win32 rejects it in a directory name outright, and Git Bash silently strips it, so it would appear to work in one shell and be quietly wrong in the other.

The five existing skills keep their bare names **for now**. Renaming them breaks existing installs, rewrites `skills-lock.json` keys, and has to move the by-name cross-references in `pr-review-followup`'s body together — different blast radius, so it gets its own PR.

## Eval design

The suite asserts on **real commit objects** read back with git, not on a log of intercepted calls, because for this skill the commits *are* the output. Nothing is stubbed and nothing needs to be: git is the tool under observation and the repositories

title: Feature - Add split-work for separating tangled commits and branches
text:
## Description

Separating tangled work into coherent commits or branches is done with
destructive commands, from memory, usually while trying to get something else
finished. This session did it once — splitting the `create-pr` fixes off another
branch — and the sequence was cherry-pick, `reset --hard`, `--force-with-lease`,
then a `git branch -d` that refused for a reason that had to be diagnosed before
it was safe to force. Every step there can lose work silently.

`split-work` makes it a procedure. It records a rescue point before touching
anything, refuses to start a destructive split with a dirty tree (uncommitted
work has no reflog), and verifies the result: **`git diff <rescue-sha> HEAD` must
be empty**. A pure split produces the same tree it started with, so anything
printed there means content was lost or invented, and the skill stops rather
than offering to push.

Interactive git cannot run in an agent context — `git rebase -i` and
`git add -p` need an editor or a TTY — so the skill carries non-interactive
equivalents, each verified: `reset --soft` to split a commit,
`git apply --cached --unidiff-zero` to stage a hunk, cherry-pick by SHA to split
a branch, and `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash` for a fixup
chain.

**The finding that shaped the skill is counterintuitive enough to state
plainly:**

> Running `git fetch` before `git push --force-with-lease` defeats the lease.

The lease compares the remote against your *remote-tracking ref*, and fetching
updates the very value being checked. Verified in a two-clone fixture: while the
tracking ref is stale the push is rejected with `stale info`; after a plain
`git fetch` the identical push succeeds and the other person's commit is gone
from the remote. "Fetch first to be safe" is exactly backwards. The skill checks
divergence with `git ls-remote`, which reads the remote without touching the
tracking ref, and treats the lease as a backstop rather than the check.

**Writing the tests caught a

4. STATUS: AMBER — agents asked to produce N commits from one file edit must fall back to bash (sandbox-blocked)
5. INTEL: Current staging is file-level atomic; no way to stage lines 1-50 separately from lines 51-100 within one tool call
6. EXECUTION: Extend CommitEntrySchema with `stage.hunks` supporting line-range syntax; implement via git diff + git apply --cached

8. COMMS: Document hunk feature in README + mcp-tools.md; link to atomic-staging semantics doc
9. HIGHER: Unblocks agents needing fine-grained commit granularity without bash fallback

## SITUATION

From `TODO.md`: batch_commit stages whole files atomically. Agents asked to produce N commits from a single-file edit cannot split post-hoc (sandbox blocks `git reset --soft`; `git rebase -i` is interactive).

Requested interface:
```typescript

  stage: { hunks: [{ file: "Makefile", lines: "120-180" }] },
  message: "feat(make): add sbom target"
})
```

title: :sparkles: feat: split hunks into smaller chunks
text:
## What

Adds hunk splitting to `gah` — the non-interactive equivalent of `git add -p`'s **split** (`s`) and **edit** (`e`) modes.

### `--split` (on `preview` and `add`)
Re-diffs at zero context (`-U0`) so git's merged hunks break into the smallest separable pieces, each with its own stable anchor. Applied with `git apply --unidiff-zero` (plain apply rejects zero-context patches).

```bash
gah preview src/main.rs --split        # finest-grained hunks
gah add src/main.rs --split -a Beast   # stage one split-out change
```

### `--lines` → partial-hunk staging
Now trims a matched hunk to only the changed lines within the range — including a **single line out of an adjacent replacement block**, which git (and `--split`) cannot separate.

```bash
gah add src/main.rs --lines 142        # one line out of a multi-line edit
```

Grouped remove/add runs (git emits `-b -c -d +B +C +D`, not interleaved) are paired positionally so kept changes land in the correct new-file order.

## Breaking change

`--lines` previously staged **every hunk overlapping** the range; it now stages **only the changed lines within** the range. Pass a range covering the whole hunk to recover the old behavior. Flagged in CHANGELOG. (Pre-1.0, low blast radius.)

## Design notes

- `--lines` keeps default U3 context (not U0): zero-context single insertions get misplaced by `git apply --unidiff-zero` (appended instead of positioned). Surrounding context anchors them.
- Adjacent changed lines can't be `--split` apart — git keeps them in one hunk even at U0. `--lines` is the tool for those. Documented in README + SKILL.md.

## Tests

- 4 unit tests for `restrict_to_lines` (replacement-middle, range, no-change-in-range, insertion).
- 5 integration tests (split-separate, split-stage-one, lines-single-line-in-block, lines-single-insertion, lines-no-match).
- All green: 25 tests pass, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` clean, `cargo fmt --check` clean.

## Summary

Adds a branch-by-branch characterization suite for `gitNoRepoAutomationEnvForLocalRepo`, the git config discovery that untrusted projects run before every local bash command and worktree operation. This is the first of two stacked PRs for #4661. The second PR replaces the four sequential `git` spawns with one shell spawn and has to keep these cases green.

## Background

Discovery is a security control: it refuses repo config that command-scope env cannot neutralize, and it lists the drivers and commands to blank out. The current tests cover a few driver classes but not the non-repository, worktree-config, refusal-scope or git-failure branches. Changing how discovery spawns git without pinning those first would leave the swap unreviewable.

## Implementation

  - A PATH-first `git` shim injects failures that real repositories cannot produce (non-128 rev-parse exits, a killed rev-parse, failing worktree/unrepresentable/driver queries) and records the exact queries and `LC_ALL` per step.

title: 🤖 perf: inspect untrusted repo automation config with one spawn
text:
## Summary

In untrusted projects, `gitNoRepoAutomationEnvForLocalRepo` runs before every local `workspace.executeBash` and before untrusted worktree create/fork. It used to spawn 4 sequential `git` processes (5 with `extensions.worktreeConfig=true`) from the Electron main process. Now it makes **one** `execFileAsync` of a POSIX shell script that runs the same git queries and reports each exit status in-band. There is no caching or sharing between callers, so every call still takes its own snapshot.

## Background

Each spawn from the main process forks the large Electron process and blocks its thread for about 8–16 ms. #4624 measured 20 main-process forks per untrusted cold open (16 of them from discovery), landing inside the chat replay. #4675 already moved the workspace-open probes after caught-up. This PR removes the remaining per-call fork cost: 4 forks become 1 per discovery, so an untrusted cold open should drop from 20 main-process spawns to 8 (measured in a comment below).

Stack: #4678 (characterization tests, merged) → #4704 (include-following fix, merged) → this PR.

## Implementation

- **Spawn.** `/bin/sh -c <script>` on POSIX, and Git Bash via `getBashPath()` on Windows, using the same argument channel as `LocalBaseRuntime.exec`. Only the repo path and the two patterns are interpolated, via `shellQuote`. Every call is `command git -C "$repo" …` with the previous argv and per-query `LC_ALL`. The cwd is inherited, and `BASH_ENV` is blanked.
- **Framing.** stdout is `HEADER + PAYLOAD + NUL + RECORD + LF`.
  - Only the driver query streams repo-controlled bytes, and it runs last.
  - The record after the last NUL is written after the last git call exits, and the script exits 0 only after writing it.
  - The exported `parseLocalRepoAutomationDiscovery` maps each record to the previous outcomes, with the same error messages and the same refusal cause chain.
  - Any spawn failure, signal, timeout, abort, output overflow or malformed output throws the automat

text:
## Summary

Adds automated Markdown formatting so that agent edits and manual edits stay consistently formatted without leaving cleanup work after every commit.

**Problem**: After the #146 merge, formatting changes (blank lines after headings, table column normalization) were waiting for commit because VS Code's formatter applied them but agents didn't. Any human or agent edit to a `.md` file risked triggering the same follow-up formatting noise.

**Solution**: Three-layer auto-format approach:

1. **Pre-commit hook** (`.githooks/pre-commit`) — runs `markdownlint-cli2 --fix` on every staged `.md` file before commit and re-stages the result. Never blocks commits. Covers all committed changes regardless of source (agent or human).
2. **`formatOnSave: true`** (`.vscode/settings.json`) — VS Code formats on save for markdown (blank lines, table normalization via Prettier extension). Covers the interactive editing experience.
3. **Agent quick-validate instructions** (`.github/copilot-instructions.md` + `CLAUDE.md`) — `markdownlint-cli2 --fix "**/*.md"` is now the first step in quick-validate, so agents run it before structural checks.

text:
## Summary

Batch of 4 small fixes — single commit, all validated.

## Changes

### #152 + #153 — `.githooks/pre-commit`

**#152**: The hook unconditionally re-staged the full working-tree file after markdownlint, defeating `git add -p` partial staging. Fixed by only re-staging if markdownlint actually changed the file (hash-object comparison).

**#153**: `git add "$f"` lacked the `--` end-of-options separator. A filename beginning with `-` would be parsed as a flag. Fixed by using `git add -- "$f"`.

Combined fix (3-line change):
```sh
_hash_before=$(git hash-object -- "$f")
markdownlint-cli2 --fix "$f" || true
_hash_after=$(git hash-object -- "$f")
[ "$_hash_before" != "$_hash_after" ] && git add -- "$f"
```

title: fix(deps): suppress LabJack stdout during import to fix CLI output contamination
text:
## Problem

The `sweep` CLI command was producing contaminated output, causing test failures in `test_cli_sweep.py`. When LabJackPython fails to load the Exodriver (a common scenario in environments without the USB driver), it prints warnings directly to stdout during module import:

```
<class 'LabJackPython.LabJackException'>: Could not load the Exodriver driver. Ethernet connectivity only.

Check that the Exodriver is installed, and the permissions are set correctly.
The error message was: liblabjackusb.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
```

This output appeared before the actual sweep results, breaking:
- CLI tests that parse numeric output
- Shell pipelines expecting clean frequency lists
- Any automation scripts relying on the sweep command

**Example of broken behavior:**
```bash
$ amp-benchkit sweep --start 10 --stop 100 --points 3 --mode linear
<class 'LabJackPython.LabJackException'>: Could not load the Exodriver driver...
10
55
100
```

## Solution

Modified `amp_benchkit/deps.py` to temporarily redirect stdout to `/dev/null` during the `import u3` statement, then restore it immediately afterward. This approach:

- ✅ Ensures CLI commands produce clean stdout suitable for piping
- ✅ Allows the import to succeed/fail appropriately based on driver availability
- ✅ Preserves error information in the `U3_ERR` variable for diagnostic purposes
- ✅ Has no impact on GUI functionality or other features
- ✅ Follows the project's minimal-change guidelines (14 lines added, 1 removed)

**After the fix:**
```bash
$ amp-benchkit sweep --start 10 --stop 100 --points 3 --mode linear
10
55
100

$ for f in $(amp-benchkit sweep --start 100 --stop 1000 --points 3 --mode log); do
    echo "Frequency: $f Hz"
  done
Frequency: 100 Hz
Frequency: 316.227766 Hz
Frequency: 1000 Hz
```

title: Fix LabJackPython stdout pollution breaking sweep CLI output
text:
## Problem

The `amp-benchkit sweep` command was producing polluted output that broke its parseable format and caused test failures. When the command ran, it would output:

```bash
$ amp-benchkit sweep --start 10 --stop 100 --points 5 --mode linear
<class 'LabJackPython.LabJackException'>: Could not load the Exodriver driver. Ethernet connectivity only.

Check that the Exodriver is installed, and the permissions are set correctly.
The error message was: liblabjackusb.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
10
32.5
55
77.5
100
```

This made the output unparseable for shell pipelines and caused `test_cli_sweep.py` tests to fail when trying to parse the output as floats.

## Root Cause

The `u3` module from LabJackPython prints a multi-line warning message directly to **stdout** (not stderr) during import when the Exodriver native library isn't available. Since the module is imported in `amp_benchkit/deps.py` at the top level, this warning appeared before any CLI command output.

## Solution

Modified `amp_benchkit/deps.py` to temporarily redirect stdout to `/dev/null` during the `u3` import:

```python
# Before:
try:
    import u3 as _u3
    HAVE_U3 = True
except Exception as e:
    _u3 = None
    U3_ERR = e
    HAVE_U3 = False

# After:
try:
    # LabJackPython prints to stdout on import failure; suppress to keep CLI clean
    import os
    import sys
    _old_stdout = sys.stdout
    try:
        with open(os.devnull, 'w') as devnull:
            sys.stdout = devnull
            import u3 as _u3
            HAVE_U3 = True
    finally:
        sys.stdout = _old_stdout
except Exception as e:
    _u3 = None
    U3_ERR = e
    HAVE_U3 = False
```

## Results

The sweep command now produces clean, parseable output:

```bash
$ amp-benchkit sweep --start 10 --stop 100 --points 5 --mode linear
10
32.5
55
77.5
100

# Works in shell pipelines
$ for f in $(amp-benchkit sweep --start 50 --stop 500 --points 4 --mode linear); do
    echo "Measure at $f Hz"
d

**Purpose**: Set up all worktrees for a swarm session

#!/bin/bash
# Usage: ./create-swarm-worktrees.sh <pattern> <num-agents>

PATTERN=${1:-hierarchical}  # hierarchical | swarm | hybrid

case $PATTERN in

    # Create supervisor worktree

title: Make bulk Antigravity add resilient to UI changes
text:
## What / why

The original script used full-DOM Tailwind CSS chains (e.g. `body > div.flex.h-screen… > a:nth-child(2)`) that break on any 9Router markup change, assumed a fixed Google DOM (`#identifierNext > div > button > span`, etc.), grabbed the OAuth tab via last-tab heuristic, and deleted the `akun.txt` line even when the add failed.

This PR makes the automation resilient while keeping the same CLI (`node bot.js`) and `email|password` file format.

## Changes

- **Stable selectors**: provider/antigravity nav via `a[href=…]`, Add/Risk buttons via visible-text matching instead of class chains.
- **Risk Notice modal**: pre-confirms `ag_risk_confirmed` in localStorage + clicks through “I Understand, Continue” if it appears (old code referenced an invalid `button ::-p-text` selector that always threw).
- **Direct navigation**: goes straight to `dashboard/providers/antigravity`, falls back to sidebar clicks if no Add button renders.
- **Google flow**: account-chooser support, email/password fallback selectors, Next-button fallbacks, consent loop (Allow/Continue/I understand…) with hard-fail on wrong password, 2FA/phone challenge, and “browser may not be secure”.
- **Correct popup handling**: waits for the opener-target OAuth popup instead of assuming the last tab.
- **Verified success**: checks `/api/providers` for the antigravity connection before removing the line from `akun.txt`; failures stay in the file for retry. Per-account try/finally browser cleanup, `ok/total` summary.
- **Config**: `TARGET_URL` (arg or env) and `HEADLESS` overrides, longer timeouts, `--no-sandbox` flags.
- **Hygiene**: untracks `akun.txt` (was committed as an empty file but stayed tracked despite `.gitignore`) and adds `akun.example.txt`; local empty `akun.txt` remains ignored.

title: Add ticket number to git commit automatically
text:
---
date: 2017-01-09
title: Add ticket number to git commit automatically
summary: I'm gonna explain automation to add ticket number in your git commit
slug: add-ticket-number-to-git-commit-automatically
lang: en-US
tags: [git]
---

Most of ticket tracker like Github, pivotal tracker have function to connect your commit to ticket(story).
But every time when you commit copy and paste that of ticket number is annoy...

So I created a script using git hook to add ticket number to your commit automatically.

## Script

```bash
$ mkdir -p ~/.git-templates/hooks
$ touch ~/.git-templates/hooks/prepare-commit-msg
$ chmod u+x ~/.git-templates/hooks/prepare-commit-msg
```

Then you can copy & paste this script to `prepare-commit-msg`

```bash
#!/bin/sh

LF=$'\\\x0A'
BRANCH_NAME=$(git symbolic-ref --short HEAD)

if [[ $BRANCH_NAME =~ .*\/[0-9]* ]]; then
  PREFIX=$(echo $BRANCH_NAME | sed -e 's/\(.*\)\/\([0-9]*\)/\1/')
  NUMBER=$(echo $BRANCH_NAME | sed -e 's/\(.*\)\/\([0-9]*\)/\2/')
  if [ $PREFIX = 'story' ]; then
      MESSAGE="[#$NUMBER]"
  else
      MESSAGE="GH-$NUMBER"
  fi
  if [ $NUMBER ]; then
    sed -i.back "1s/^/$LF$LF$MESSAGE$LF/" "$1"
  fi
fi
```

## Configuration

To enable this script run this command.

```bash
$ git config core.hooksPath ~/.git-templates/hooks/
```

## Usage

This script expects that your branch is named using this format

### Pivotal Tracker

```bash
story/1111
```


### Github

```bash
issue/1111
fix/1111
feature/1111
```


When every time you commit script add that number using this format to you commit !!


### Pivotal Tracker
```bash
[#1111]
```

### Github
```bash
GH-1111
```

title: docs(gates): the partial-stage warning in lefthook.yml is false
text:
## What is wrong today

`lefthook.yml:28-34` carries this warning next to the `format` job:

> Caveat — `stage_fixed` re-stages a reformatted file with a plain `git add`, which stages
> the file *whole*. So on a partially-staged file (`git add -p`) that Prettier rewrites,
> the unstaged hunks are swept into the commit too — their content, not merely their
> formatting. Unlike lint-staged, lefthook does not stash the unstaged half first. Commit
> a partial stage of an already-formatted file, or stash the rest before committing.

**Every sentence of that is false against the lefthook this repository pins.**

Reproduced in a throwaway repository using this repo's own pinned lefthook (2.1.12, per
`package.json:58` and `pnpm-lock.yaml`) and its own prettier, with the `format` job copied
verbatim from `lefthook.yml:35-37`:

- index blob: `const a   =   1;\nconst b = 2;` (badly formatted, staged)
- worktree: `const a   =   1;\nconst b = 999; // UNSTAGED_SWEEP_MARKER`

After `git commit` the hook ran and the **committed blob was
`const a = 1;\nconst b = 2;`** — formatted, and without the unstaged marker. The worktree
kept `const b = 999; // UNSTAGED_SWEEP_MARKER`, formatted, with `git status --short`
showing ` M file.js`. Run twice, the second time with untruncated output. lefthook 2.x
hides the unstaged half around a `stage_fixed` job, exactly the way lint-staged does.

The comment was almost certainly true when written — `lefthook.yml` was last touched in
`e0595d6`, before the 2.x bump.

## Why it matters

This is not a harmless stale comment. It is load-bearing advice in the file that defines
this repository's only mechanical enforcement layer, and it tells every author — human or
agent — to avoid `git add -p`, which is the workflow that produces reviewable commits. It
also misdescribes what the layer does, in a file AGENTS.md points at as the authority.

And because the correct behaviour is now a property of a **devDependency version** rather
than something visible in t

title: chore(skills): require a dedicated worktree per change
text:
## Summary

Every change in this repository now gets its own git worktree, so several features can run in parallel without sharing the main checkout. The convention already existed in practice — `git worktree list` shows 15 worktrees under the sibling directory — but it was unwritten, so it drifted: inconsistent directory names, branches created from other worktrees' branches, and edits landing in the main checkout while another change was in flight.

## Scope

Included: the new project skill and its row in the skill index.

Explicitly excluded:

- No gate line is added to the workflow gates in `AGENTS.md`. Registered skills are loaded through their activation contract, which is how `go-tests`, `ux-ui`, and `e2e-playwright` already work; only `issue-governance` carries its own gate, because it is the blocking one.
- No helper script: this repository has no `scripts` directory, and `pr-governance` says so explicitly.
- No teardown automation, no CI change, no Go change.

## Changes

- `.agents/skills/worktree-isolation/SKILL.md` (new, 56 lines): one change, one worktree, one branch in the sibling directory next to the repository root; `issue-<n>-<slug>` directory and `<type>/<n>-<slug>` branch based on an updated `origin/main`; the `git worktree add --track` command; `mkdir -p data`; and a per-worktree `TKT_LISTEN` and `TKT_DB_PATH`.
- `AGENTS.md`: one row in the local skills index.

title: feat(worktree): managed-workspace lifecycle — persisted ownership + explicit release, startup reconciliation, and safe content-proven retirement (incl. adopted worktrees and PR-delivered work)
text:
**feat(worktree): managed-workspace lifecycle — persisted ownership + explicit release, startup reconciliation, and safe content-proven retirement (incl. adopted worktrees and PR-delivered work)**

# Summary

OMP cleans up the workspaces it creates for **task isolation**, and `omp worktree list|clear` scans a single configured directory. Nothing in OMP owns the lifecycle of a *worktree that did real work and was delivered through a pull request*. Such worktrees are created by `git worktree add` in bash (or `omp worktree add`), used by one or more sessions/subagents, merged on GitHub (often squash/rebase), and then stay on disk indefinitely. There is no record of who owns them, no notion of "released", no restart reconciliation, and no way to prove "this tree's content is already on the target" before removing it.

This is not a request for OMP to create top-level worktrees (that is #452/#6630 territory) and not a request for age/count-based auto-deletion. It is a narrow contract for **ownership, release, reconciliation and proof-gated retirement**.

# Problem

1. **Task isolation cleans only its own workspaces.** The isolation runner tears down sandboxes it created (and #13202 documents that crash leftovers and `.retained-*` dirs are manual-only). That lifecycle is tied to the task runner and an owner marker written by the isolation code. A worktree created any other way never gets a marker, so it is outside every cleanup path.

2. **Worktrees created via bash or `omp worktree add` have no ownership, release or retirement.** With `worktree.clone` off, nothing rewrites `git worktree add`; with it on, the rewrite is a creation optimization only. In both cases OMP records no (session/agent → workspace) binding, so it cannot say who is still using a tree, when the owner is done, or whether the work was delivered. I request an action, and it only takes effect if someone else repeats it. The problem though is priming, and a two key system only fixes that the first couple times. In a year you re right back where you started. Because once I ve suggested a course of action to you, the Primacy Effect makes you key your counterproposals to my initial bid, and if I m enough off the mark we end up off the mark together. Add Recency Effect on top of it - if I haven t been wrong the last ten times I asked you to spot me, you slowly stop assuming I m wrong this time. When the production outage happens, it comes out that your thought process was that I know what I m doing and you didn t need to be there for the last five times so you ve zoned out and didn t catch my mistake. And if I start my ask by sending you a URL, if I cut and pasted the wrong URL you re stuck looking at the wrong thing with me and we both sail off into the canyon together. Still, if I m careful to give you only the high-level request, and we derive the same solution from that request, then maybe a tool like that would still be useful. But the most important part of that interaction is still outside of the scope of any tool that could sanity check us. It s just process.
